chapter: Young players, Coltrane and the avant-garde
title: Avant-garde players who missed the point, Sunny Murray and the cymbal
summary: Ridley tells of a saxophonist standing silent at the Half Note and Sunny Murray's long wait to hit the cymbal.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: That was the interesting thing about it, like it...those guys who were coming on the scene then, and how, how could they sit there and look and see him doing that kind of thing and hear what he was doing and just miss the boat?
And just be so ready just jump up on

the stage--I met him one night, uh, Wayne's brother Allan-- Super hit, Superfly--jumped up on the stage one night down at the Half Note and that fool stood up there for about a half hour and he played nary a note. Standing up there trying to get ready to try and play something, you know, like if something like, somethings happening to the rhythm section or something he he go to put the horn up, getting ready to like he's...lead...make a face. I mean every- thing was drama, you know, so theatrics and he took the horn down and he started rubbing his ear and look around at the rhythm section like something was bugging him, you know. And this nigger ain't playing shit, you know. I said wait a minute, man. And I'll never forget one night Sunny Murray was down there sitting there on the drums, and he's up there and you know how he'd be with that stuff he'd be doing, he get a little bit that he's up in here, and then, then one time he just sat up there for about five minutes and he never would hit the cymbals. So, finally, I was sitting up here on the side right by the jukebox, you know how the jukebox up against the window--so finally it just frustrated me so much I just, I just said, "Nigger hit the cymbal!" (Laughter). As I asked him as he came off the stage, I said, "what was all that shit all about, you know." He said, "well, you know, sometimes it ain't always right on the cymbal, it could be up in there, you know." Like the beat is wide, you know, like he waited till some old cosmic stuff he was running down, you know.

I said 'but how do you do that, you know, on a record date?' See he wasn't doing nothing but making disco bigger. See that's the same thing I was trying to say, tell you when I seen the laymen is sitting out there in the audience. Do you understand what I mean? So he's sitting out there and he's trying, you see, god damn man. See but now it could see. And the record sales, oh man see the jazz record sales was big man. Because they go and buy up all the records. They take their share home man. And so he would stay home. But now when they had the big beat horns, the big back beat, you see.
